'''''Divina proportione''''' (15th century Italian for ''Divine proportion''), later also called '''''De divina proportione''''' (converting the Italian title into a Latin one) is a book on mathematics written by [[Luca Pacioli]] and illustrated by [[Leonardo da Vinci]], completed by February 9th, 1498<ref>{{Cite web|title=Tennenbaum Pacioli-Divine-Proportion PDF {{!}} PDF {{!}} Axiom {{!}} Geometry|url=https://www.scribd.com/document/244035060/tennenbaum-pacioli-divine-proportion-pdf|access-date=2022-02-08|website=Scribd|language=en}}</ref> in [[Milan]] and first printed in 1509.<ref name="StAnd"/> Its subject was [[Mathematics and art|mathematical proportions]] (the title refers to the [[golden ratio]]) and their applications to geometry, to visual art through [[Perspective (graphical)|perspective]], and [[mathematics and architecture|to architecture]]. The clarity of the written material and Leonardo's excellent diagrams helped the book to achieve an impact beyond mathematical circles, popularizing contemporary geometric concepts and images.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.georgehart.com/virtual-polyhedra/pacioli.html|title=Luca Pacioli's Polyhedra|first=George W.|last=Hart|website=Virtual Polyhedra|access-date=23 January 2015}}</ref><ref name=Y>{{Cite web|url = http://www.math.ubc.ca/~hoek/Teaching/Golden/Divina.html|publisher = [[University of British Columbia]]|title = The Rose and the Nautilus|last = Hoechsmann|first = Klaus Hoechsmann|date = 1 April 2001|access-date = 15 January 2015}}</ref>

Some of its content was [[plagiarism|plagiarised]] from an earlier book by [[Piero della Francesca]], ''[[De quinque corporibus regularibus]]''.

==Contents of the book==
{{further|Mathematics and art}}
The book consists of three separate manuscripts,<ref name="StAnd">{{Cite web|url = http://www-history.mcs.st-and.ac.uk/Biographies/Pacioli.html|title = Luca Pacioli|website = School of Mathematics and Statistics|publisher = [[University of St Andrews]]|last1 = O'Connor|first1 = J J|last2 = Robertson|first2 = E F|date = July 1999|access-date = 15 January 2015}}</ref> which Pacioli worked on between 1496 and 1498. He credits [[Fibonacci]] as the main source for the mathematics he presents.{{sfn|Livio|2003|p=130}}

===''Compendio divina proportione''===
The first part, ''Compendio divina proportione'' (''Compendium on the Divine Proportion''), studies the [[golden ratio]] from a mathematical perspective (following the relevant work of [[Euclid]]), giving mystical and religious meanings to this ratio, in seventy-one chapters.<ref name="StAnd"/> Pacioli points out that [[:File:Icosahedron-golden-rectangles.svg|golden rectangles can be inscribed by an icosahedron]],{{sfn|Livio|2003|p=132}} and in the fifth chapter, gives five reasons why the golden ratio should be referred to as the "Divine Proportion":{{sfn|Livio|2003|pp=130, 131}}
#Its value represents [[divine simplicity]].
#Its definition invokes three lengths, symbolizing the [[Holy Trinity]].
#Its [[Irrational number|irrationality]] represents God's incomprehensibility.
#Its [[self-similarity]] recalls God's [[omnipresence]] and invariability.
#Its relation to the [[dodecahedron]], which represents the [[Aether (classical element)|quintessence]]

It also contains a discourse on the [[Regular polyhedra|regular]] and [[semiregular polyhedra]],<ref name=E/><ref>{{Cite journal|first=J F|last=Field|title=Rediscovering the Archimedean polyhedra: Piero della Francesca, Luca Pacioli, Leonardo da Vinci, Albrecht Dürer, Daniele Barbaro, and Johannes Kepler|journal=Arch. Hist. Exact Sci.|volume=50|number=3–4|year=1997|pages=241–289|doi=10.1007/BF00374595 |s2cid=118516740 }}</ref> as well as a discussion of the use of [[geometric perspective]] by painters such as [[Piero della Francesca]], [[Melozzo da Forlì]] and [[Marco Palmezzano]].
[[File:Pacioli De Divina Proportione Head Equilateral Triangle 1509.jpg|thumb|Woodcut illustrating proportions of the human face]]

===''Trattato dell'architettura''===
The second part, ''Trattato dell'architettura'' (''Treatise on Architecture''), discusses the ideas of [[Vitruvius]] (from his ''[[De architectura]]'') on the application of [[mathematics and architecture|mathematics to architecture]] in twenty chapters. The text compares the proportions of the human body to those of artificial structures, with examples from classical [[Greco-Roman world#Architecture|Greco-Roman architecture]].

===''Libellus in tres partiales divisus''===
The third part, ''Libellus in tres partiales divisus'' (''Book divided into three parts''), is a translation into Italian of [[Piero della Francesca]]'s Latin book ''[[De quinque corporibus regularibus]]'' [''On [the] Five Regular Solids''].<ref name="StAnd"/><ref name=E>{{Cite web |url=http://ww3.ac-poitiers.fr/arts_p/b@lise14/pageshtm/page_4.htm |title=La Divine Proportion de Luca Pacioli |language=fr |publisher=Académie de Poitiers |last=Gardes |first=Michel |date=20 June 2001 |access-date=15 January 2015 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150127090823/http://ww3.ac-poitiers.fr/arts_p/b%40lise14/pageshtm/page_4.htm |archive-date=27 January 2015 }}</ref> It does not credit della Francesca for this material, and in 1550 [[Giorgio Vasari]] wrote a biography of della Francesca, in which he accused Pacioli of plagiarism and claimed that he stole della Francesca's work on perspective, on arithmetic and on geometry.<ref name="StAnd"/> Because della Francesca's book had been lost, these accusations remained unsubstantiated until the 19th century, when a copy of della Francesca's book was found in the [[Vatican Library]] and a comparison confirmed that Pacioli had copied it.<ref>{{cite book
 | last = Davis | first = Margaret Daly
 | pages = 98–99
 | publisher = Longo Editore
 | title = Piero Della Francesca's Mathematical Treatises: The Trattato D'abaco and Libellus de Quinque Corporibus Regularibus
 | url = https://archive.org/details/PieroDellaFrancescasMathematicalTreatises
 | year = 1977}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal
 | last = Peterson | first = Mark A.
 | doi = 10.1007/BF03025346
 | issue = 3
 | journal = The Mathematical Intelligencer
 | mr = 1475147
 | pages = 33–40
 | title = The geometry of Piero della Francesca
 | volume = 19
 | year = 1997| s2cid = 120720532
 }}</ref>

===Illustrations===
<!--[[File:Leonardo polyhedra.png|thumb|240px|The first printed illustration of a [[rhombicuboctahedron]], by [[Leonardo da Vinci]].]]-->
After these three parts are appended two sections of illustrations, the first showing twenty-three capital letters drawn with a ruler and compass by Pacioli and the second with some sixty illustrations in [[woodcut]] after drawings by [[Leonardo da Vinci]].<ref name=X>{{Cite web|url=http://www.metmuseum.org/works_of_art/collection_database/drawings_and_prints/divina_proportione_leonardo_da_vinci/objectview.aspx?collID=9&OID=90003660|website = The Collection Online|publisher = Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York|title = Divina proportione, after Leonardo da Vinci|access-date = 15 January 2015}}</ref> Leonardo drew the illustrations of the regular solids while he lived with and took mathematics lessons from Pacioli. Leonardo's drawings are probably the first illustrations of skeletonic solids which allowed an easy distinction between front and back.

Another collaboration between Pacioli and Leonardo existed: Pacioli planned a book of mathematics and [[proverb]]s called ''De Viribus Quantitatis'' (''The powers of numbers'')<ref>{{cite thesis|author=Tiago Hirth |title=Luca Pacioli and his 1500 book De Viribus Quantitatis' |url=https://repositorio.ul.pt/bitstream/10451/18435/1/ulfc113829_tm_Tiago_Hirth.pdf |location=University of Lisbon |language=pt |degree=MA |year=2015}}</ref> which Leonardo was to illustrate, but Pacioli died before he could publish it.{{sfn|Livio|2003|p=137}}

==History==
Pacioli produced three manuscripts of the treatise by different scribes. He gave the first copy with a dedication to the Duke of Milan, [[Ludovico il Moro]]; this manuscript is now preserved in Switzerland at the [[Bibliothèque Publique et Universitaire (Geneva)|Bibliothèque de Genève]] in Geneva. A second copy was donated to [[Galeazzo da Sanseverino]] and now rests at the [[Biblioteca Ambrosiana]] in Milan. On 1 June 1509 the first printed edition was published in Venice by [[Paganino Paganini]];<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia|title=PAGANINI, Paganino|encyclopedia=Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani|language=it|volume=80|year=2014|last=Nuovo|first=Angela|publisher=Treccani|url=http://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/paganino-paganini_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/|access-date=27 January 2015}}</ref> it has since been reprinted several times.

[[File:Fra Luca Pacioli Letter M 1509.png|thumb|Architectural letter 'M']]
The book was displayed as part of an exhibition in Milan between October 2005 and October 2006 together with the [[Codex Atlanticus]].<ref>{{Cite web|url = https://www.leonardo3.net/leonardo/atlantico/manoscritti_eng.htm|title = The Virtual Codex Atlanticus|website = Leonardo3|access-date = 15 January 2015|archive-date = 3 March 2016|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160303232429/https://www.leonardo3.net/leonardo/atlantico/manoscritti_eng.htm|url-status = dead}}</ref> The "M" logo used by the [[Metropolitan Museum of Art]] in New York was adapted from one in ''Divina proportione''.<ref name=T>{{Cite web|url = http://store.metmuseum.org/magnets-bookmarks+novelties/renaissance-m-bookmark/invt/10086668/|website = The Met Store|publisher = Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York|title = Renaissance 'M' Bookmark|access-date = 15 January 2015}}</ref>
